<!--     The single sentence a hiring manager should remember.          -->
::: {.result-banner}
Cut voluntary churn 18% by targeting only the users a save-offer could actually persuade — worth ~$2.4M in retained ARR.
:::

<!-- 2 ── PROBLEM — 3 sentences, business framing --------------------- -->
## The problem

Retention was blanket-emailing every at-risk account a 20% discount, which was expensive and, for many users, unnecessary. The business needed to know *who* to spend the offer on, not just who was likely to leave. The distinction matters because the biggest churn-risk group includes people who will churn regardless — and people who'd have stayed anyway.

<!-- 3 ── HERO CHART — the visual that IS the finding ----------------- -->
## The finding

```{python}
#| label: fig-hero
#| fig-cap: "Uplift decile vs. realized retention lift. Only the top ~40% of users are persuadable; the bottom deciles are neutral-to-negative."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Replace this synthetic series with your real evaluation output.
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
deciles = np.arange(1, 11)
uplift = np.array([9.5, 7.8, 5.9, 3.6, 1.9, 0.7, 0.1, -0.4, -1.1, -1.8]) + rng.normal(0, 0.2, 10)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
colors = ["#2563eb" if u > 0 else "#c0c4cc" for u in uplift]
ax.bar(deciles, uplift, color=colors)
ax.axhline(0, color="#1f2328", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Predicted-uplift decile (10 = most persuadable)")
ax.set_ylabel("Retention lift (pp)")
ax.set_xticks(deciles)
for s in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color("#d5d5df"); ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#d5d5df")
ax.grid(axis="y", color="#eef0f4", lw=1)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Targeting the blue deciles and skipping the grey ones is the whole result: same budget, better spent.

<!-- 4 ── DECISIONS & TRADEOFFS — 2 paragraphs, incl. what FAILED ----- -->
## Decisions and tradeoffs

I framed this as uplift (treatment-effect) modeling rather than churn prediction — a deliberate choice, because a well-calibrated churn model still can't tell you whether the offer *changed* anyone's behavior. I used a two-model T-learner over gradient-boosted trees, evaluated with the Qini coefficient on a held-out randomized slice. Keeping a genuine randomized holdout cost us some offers we "knew" were good, but without it there is no honest way to measure uplift.

The first approach failed: a single S-learner with treatment as a feature collapsed the uplift signal — the treatment coefficient was swamped by the far stronger churn features, and predicted uplift was near-flat across deciles. Switching to separate treatment/control models recovered the signal. I also tried a causal forest, which matched the T-learner on Qini but was slower to retrain and harder to explain to the retention team, so I shipped the simpler model.

<!-- 5 ── MEASUREMENT + HONEST LIMITATIONS --------------------------- -->
## Measurement and limitations

Success was measured on the randomized holdout: retention lift by uplift decile (the chart above) and the Qini coefficient (0.21 vs. 0.0 for random targeting). Two honest limitations: the model is trained on one offer type (20% discount), so uplift estimates won't transfer to a different intervention without re-randomizing; and the top decile is thin, so its point estimate carries wide confidence intervals. I'd re-run the holdout quarterly to catch drift as the user mix changes.

## How it works

The core of the T-learner and Qini evaluation:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the uplift model + Qini evaluation"
#| eval: false
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

def fit_t_learner(X, y, treated):
    """Two-model uplift: P(retain | treated) - P(retain | control)."""
    m_t = HistGradientBoostingClassifier().fit(X[treated],  y[treated])
    m_c = HistGradientBoostingClassifier().fit(X[~treated], y[~treated])
    return m_t, m_c

def predict_uplift(m_t, m_c, X):
    return m_t.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] - m_c.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]

def qini_coefficient(uplift, y, treated):
    order = uplift.argsort()[::-1]
    y, treated = y[order], treated[order]
    n_t = treated.cumsum(); n_c = (~treated).cumsum()
    gain = (y * treated).cumsum() - (y * ~treated).cumsum() * (n_t / np.maximum(n_c, 1))
    return gain / gain.size  # normalized area vs. random
```
